extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers; students of literature and philosophy; readers of Montaigne
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis/extraction of prescriptive and evaluative maxims embedded in Michel de Montaigne's essay 'Of Vanity' (translation). The page is a literary-philosophical essay offering behavioral, civic, and stylistic judgments rather than a formal rubric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vain writing about vanity
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing about vanity in a vain manner is itself the height of vanity: 'There is, peradventure, no more manifest vanity than to write of it so vainly.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When treating moral themes like vanity, adopt sincere meditation and restraint rather than self-aggrandizing or merely rhetorical treatments; aim for genuine reflection rather than empty prating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrict frivolous scribblers
rubrics_metrics.description: Scribbling and impertinent publications are a social ill and, in times of disorder, should be restrained like vagabonds: 'There should be some restraint of law against foolish and impertinent scribblers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize excessive, pointless publication as symptomatic of a licentious age; favor limiting pointless pamphleteering that distracts from more pressing public matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not neglect one's vocation for intellectual refinement
rubrics_metrics.description: Refining one's wit does not make people wiser in government and often springs from negligence toward one's proper duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid allowing literary or speculative pursuits to distract you from practical obligations and duties of your vocation; practical responsibilities should not be abandoned for refinement alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize major evils over minor concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: When great disorders or pressing harms exist, it is not the time to concern oneself with small or cosmetic reforms: 'Friend, it is not now time to play with your nails.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Triage problems: address pressing, serious evils before attending to lesser inconveniences or aesthetic reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commit fully to self-change; avoid half-measures
rubrics_metrics.description: One should not attempt to 'mend by halves'—either undertake real change or accept your state: 'I scorn to mend myself by halves.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you decide to reform habits or character, do so wholeheartedly; half-measures are inconsistent and ineffective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use fortune to temper modesty and virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Good fortune should spur modesty and moderation, while adversity often disciplines and improves conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respond to prosperity with humility and to adversity as an opportunity for moral improvement; do not equate success with moral superiority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor contentment over craving novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Those satisfied with what they have are often happier than those constantly seeking new things: 'Those who follow the other extreme... are really more happy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate contentment; avoid constant restlessness for novelty as a measure of improvement or happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance travel with domestic retirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Travel is pleasant but costly and should not spoil the pleasure of retirement; journeys should be shorter and fewer if they undermine domestic peace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan travel so it complements, not detracts from, the peace of home life; be mindful of the expense and impact on long-term contentment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Household management: prefer order and cleanliness to display
rubrics_metrics.description: Value order and cleanliness more than abundance or outward show: 'I love order and cleanliness... more than abundance.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In domestic affairs emphasize necessity and regular management rather than ostentatious display; good husbandry is valuable though not everyman’s pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Host should avoid visible fussing when entertaining
rubrics_metrics.description: A gentleman ought not to bustle over household affairs in front of guests; management should 'insensibly slide along.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When entertaining, make household arrangements appear effortless; avoid complaining or apologizing about provisions or service to guests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise measured trust and avoid micromanagement of servants
rubrics_metrics.description: The author places confidence in servants, especially younger ones, and tolerates some ignorance as security: 'The most common security I take of my people is ignorance.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delegate responsibilities with reasonable trust, accept small losses rather than obsessive oversight, and presume innocence until proven otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid obsessive scrutiny of money (avarice breeds itself)
rubrics_metrics.description: Delighting in counting and handling money is a sign of avarice; excessive study of one's money invites its approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't let handling money become a consuming habit; allow for some uncertainty and avoid constantly recounting or micromanaging funds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize practical skills over abstract reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer acquiring practical, useful skills (e.g., horsemanship) to purely speculative knowledge or reputation: 'I had rather be a good horseman than a good logician.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value competencies that serve everyday life and self-sufficiency over abstract learning pursued for vanity or status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not live for public appearance; prioritize private utility
rubrics_metrics.description: People too often live by reference to others' opinions, depriving themselves of real utility for the sake of show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange life around genuine needs and private goods rather than public approbation and appearances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation in spending; avoid artificial liberality or pinched calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: Keeping or spending money is morally neutral; systematic, overly scrupulous ordering of expense makes life too pinched; artificial liberality is also undesirable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a moderate, natural approach to expenditure rather than extreme parsimony or performative generosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid seeking public office without aptitude and means
rubrics_metrics.description: Public service is honorable but burdensome; one should abstain from public command if one lacks capacity or inclination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be realistic about ability and disposition before taking public roles; abstaining can be prudent and morally defensible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer existing, functioning government to ideal abstract models
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'best' government is the one under which a people is maintained; custom and existing institutions often suit a people better than theoretical models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging or reforming polity, recognize the stabilizing role of custom; radical replacement of institutions risks greater harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise caution with innovations; change breeds unexpected tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: Innovation and great change commonly lead to disorder or tyranny: 'Nothing presses so hard upon a state as innovation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach systemic reform cautiously; consider the risk of worse consequences following upheaval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cures must restore function, not merely remove defects
rubrics_metrics.description: Like a surgeon who must fill and heal after cutting away dead flesh, a reformer must aim to restore and improve, not only excise an offending part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design reforms to rebuild and heal institutions or situations, not merely to remove unpopular elements; consider replacement structures and long-term healing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to small domestic annoyances; they often cause deepest distress
rubrics_metrics.description: Small, constant inconveniences ('little affairs') are more piercing and disruptive than isolated major harms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not neglect the everyday small discomforts of life; their accumulation can degrade well-being markedly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that societies form even from vice; purely artificial political models are often impractical
rubrics_metrics.description: Even groups of wicked people can form a functioning polity; contrived models of government often fail when applied to real human conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of utopian political schemes divorced from human nature; ground political thought in observed practice and necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberately preserve some ignorance in affairs to reduce anxiety
rubrics_metrics.description: The author purposely harbours an uncertain knowledge of his finances to avoid constant vexation: 'I purposely, harbour a kind of perplexed, uncertain knowledge of my money.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow bounded uncertainty in nonessential matters to reduce continual worry and micromanagement; determine reasonable limits for oversight.
